slang.label: Slang Mexicano (Mexican Slang)
slang.description: Informal Mexican Spanish expressions and Jalisco regional slang

words.notes: Very common informal greeting in Mexico. More casual than '¿Cómo estás?'
words.example_es: ¿Qué onda, güey? ¿Todo bien?
words.example_en: What's up, dude? All good?

words.notes: Used as a greeting or to ask what happened. Common in Jalisco.
words.example_es: ¡Hola vecino! ¿Qué pasó?
words.example_en: Hey neighbor! What's up?

words.notes: A quick, casual greeting used any time of day throughout Mexico.
words.example_es: Buenas, ¿tiene limones?
words.example_en: Hi, do you have limes?

words.english: Pardon? / Yes? / How can I help you?
words.notes: Very Mexican polite response when you didn't hear something. More formal than '¿Qué?'
words.example_es: —Señora. —¿Mande?
words.example_en: —Ma'am. —Yes? / Pardon?

words.notes: Informal Mexican slang for beer. Very common in Jalisco social settings.
words.example_es: ¿Vamos por unas chelas al lago?
words.example_en: Shall we grab some beers by the lake?

words.notes: Jalisco's signature dish. Slow-cooked spiced meat stew, especially popular on weekends.
words.example_es: La birria de chivo de Ajijic es la mejor.
words.example_en: The goat birria from Ajijic is the best.

words.notes: A Jalisco-specialty sandwich drowned in spicy tomato-chile sauce. A must-try in the Guadalajara area.
words.example_es: Quiero una torta ahogada bien picosa.
words.example_en: I want a well-spiced drowned sandwich.

words.notes: Non-alcoholic drinks made from fruits, flowers, or seeds. Jamaica, horchata, and tamarindo are popular.
words.example_es: Una agua de jamaica, por favor.
words.example_en: A hibiscus water, please.

words.notes: In Mexico, 'elote' specifically refers to fresh corn. Street vendors called 'eloteros' are common in Ajijic.
words.example_es: El elotero pasa por la calle Morelos cada tarde.
words.example_en: The corn vendor passes by Morelos street every afternoon.

words.english: Lake Chapala / the town of Chapala
words.notes: Mexico's largest freshwater lake, adjacent to Ajijic. Also refers to the town of Chapala.
words.example_es: Voy al malecón de Chapala este fin de semana.
words.example_en: I'm going to the Chapala boardwalk this weekend.

words.notes: The lakefront walkway. Both Ajijic and Chapala have malecones—popular spots for locals and expats.
words.example_es: Caminemos por el malecón al atardecer.
words.example_en: Let's walk along the boardwalk at sunset.

words.notes: Traditional open-air market. Ajijic's tianguis (Wednesday and Saturday) is a community institution.
words.example_es: Voy al tianguis el miércoles para comprar verduras.
words.example_en: I'm going to the outdoor market on Wednesday to buy vegetables.

words.notes: In Ajijic, 'la carretera' almost always refers to the main lakeside highway (Carretera Chapala-Jocotepec).
words.example_es: El restaurante está sobre la carretera.
words.example_en: The restaurant is on the main highway.

words.notes: When locals say 'el lago' in Ajijic, they always mean Lake Chapala.
words.example_es: ¿Bajamos al lago a ver el atardecer?
words.example_en: Shall we go down to the lake to watch the sunset?

words.notes: The standard way to ask price at a market. More natural than '¿Cuánto cuesta?'
words.example_es: ¿A cuánto están los aguacates?
words.example_en: How much are the avocados?

words.english: Can you give me...? / I'll take...
words.notes: Polite way to order or request items at market stalls. More natural than 'Quiero...'
words.example_es: ¿Me da un kilo de jitomate?
words.example_en: Can I have a kilo of tomatoes?

words.english: Is there anything else? / Are you missing anything?
words.notes: Vendors commonly ask this when you're wrapping up a purchase.
words.example_es: —Aquí tiene su cambio. ¿Le falta algo? —No, gracias, ya está.
words.example_en: —Here's your change. Anything else? —No thanks, that's all.

words.notes: In Mexico, 'jitomate' is the red tomato. 'Tomate' refers to the green tomatillo.
words.example_es: Necesito jitomates para la salsa.
words.example_en: I need tomatoes for the salsa.

words.notes: Ajijic's rainy season (June–October) brings afternoon storms. The rest of the year is dry and mild.
words.example_es: Ya empezó la temporada de lluvias—hay que regar menos el jardín.
words.example_en: The rainy season has started—we need to water the garden less.

words.notes: Cold winter winds from the north that sweep across Lake Chapala, causing choppy water.
words.example_es: Hoy está soplando el norte; llévate un suéter.
words.example_en: The north wind is blowing today; bring a sweater.

words.notes: Ajijic's climate is often described as 'fresco'—pleasantly cool, the 'City of Eternal Spring' (though this is really neighboring Guadalajara's nickname).
words.example_es: Qué fresco está hoy en la mañana.
words.example_en: It's so cool/pleasant this morning.

words.notes: Ajijic has many local fiestas celebrating patron saints. The San Andrés fiesta in November is a major event.
words.example_es: La fiesta de San Andrés es en noviembre con fuegos artificiales.
words.example_en: The Saint Andrew's festival is in November with fireworks.

words.notes: Loud rockets set off during fiestas at all hours. A very common Ajijic experience!
words.example_es: Los cohetones empezaron a las 5 de la mañana otra vez.
words.example_en: The fireworks started at 5 in the morning again.

words.notes: A crew of local workers for construction or garden projects. Very commonly used in expat conversations.
words.example_es: La cuadrilla viene el lunes a pintar la barda.
words.example_en: The work crew is coming Monday to paint the wall.

words.notes: Ajijic homes often have beautiful gardens. This also refers to the town square (jardín principal).
words.example_es: Las buganvilias del jardín están floreciendo.
words.example_en: The bougainvilleas in the garden are blooming.

words.notes: A common feature of Mexican homes—the exterior masonry wall around the property.
words.example_es: Necesitamos pintar la barda antes de la temporada de lluvias.
words.example_en: We need to paint the boundary wall before the rainy season.

words.notes: Plastic water storage tanks on rooftops are common throughout Mexico including Ajijic.
words.example_es: Hay que revisar el tinaco—se puede estar acabando el agua.
words.example_en: We should check the water tank—the water might be running low.

words.notes: In Mexico, local buses are called 'camiones.' The camión runs between Ajijic and Guadalajara.
words.example_es: El camión a Guadalajara sale cada hora de la parada.
words.example_en: The bus to Guadalajara leaves every hour from the stop.

words.notes: Small shared vans running along the lake road, a cheap way to get between towns.
words.example_es: Toma la combi hasta Chapala—cuesta muy poco.
words.example_en: Take the minibus to Chapala—it costs very little.

words.notes: The most ubiquitous informal term in Mexican Spanish. Can be used between friends regardless of gender. Not offensive between friends.
words.example_es: ¡No manches, güey, qué chido!
words.example_en: No way, dude, that's so cool!

words.english: No way! / Are you serious? / Wow! (mild expletive)
words.notes: A mild exclamation used to express surprise or frustration. Family-friendly version of a stronger expression.
words.example_es: ¡No manches! ¿Ya llegó el verano?
words.example_en: No way! Has summer already arrived?

words.notes: Very common Mexican slang for something being cool or excellent.
words.example_es: Ese restaurante nuevo está bien chido.
words.example_en: That new restaurant is really cool.

words.english: Right now / In a moment / Later (context-dependent)
words.notes: One of the most important Mexican expressions to understand! Meaning depends entirely on context—could mean in a few minutes, a few hours, or never.
words.example_es: —¿Cuándo llega el plomero? —Ahorita.
words.example_en: —When does the plumber arrive? —(Soon/Later/Eventually).

words.english: Come on / Go ahead / Okay / That's right
words.notes: Extremely versatile Mexican expression used to agree, encourage, or acknowledge something.
words.example_es: —¿Nos vamos? —¡Ándale!
words.example_en: —Shall we go? —Let's go! / Alright!

words.notes: Similar to 'ándale.' Can express agreement, surprise, or encouragement. Very Jalisco/Mexican.
words.example_es: ¿Vamos al lago? ¡Órale!
words.example_en: Going to the lake? Sure!/Let's go!

words.english: Hell yeah / Absolutely / For sure (strong affirmation)
words.notes: Strong affirmative expression. Considered mild profanity—use among friends, not in formal settings.
words.example_es: —¿Ya ganó el equipo? —¡A huevo!
words.example_en: —Did the team win? —Hell yeah!

words.notes: Small-town Ajijic has plenty of chisme! An important social concept.
words.example_es: ¿Ya oíste el chisme del vecino?
words.example_en: Have you heard the gossip about the neighbor?

words.notes: Literally 'the bite.' Refers to unofficial payments to officials. Important cultural concept to understand.
words.example_es: A veces los trámites van más rápido con una mordida.
words.example_en: Sometimes paperwork goes faster with a little bribe.

words.notes: Government paperwork and procedures. Expats frequently deal with trámites for residency, car permits, etc.
words.example_es: Tengo que hacer un trámite en la delegación mañana.
words.example_en: I have to do some paperwork at the local government office tomorrow.

words.notes: Common term for foreigners, especially North Americans. Not necessarily offensive in Mexico—context matters.
words.example_es: Ajijic tiene muchos gringos que vienen a retirarse.
words.example_en: Ajijic has many foreigners who come to retire.

words.notes: Ajijic has one of the largest expat communities in Mexico, mostly retirees from the US and Canada.
words.example_es: La comunidad expat de Ajijic organiza muchos eventos.
words.example_en: The expat community in Ajijic organizes many events.

words.notes: Several clinics and hospitals serve the Ajijic/Lake Chapala area.
words.example_es: Voy a la clínica porque me duele la garganta.
words.example_en: I'm going to the clinic because my throat hurts.

words.notes: Standard term for a medical doctor. You may also hear 'doctor/doctora'.
words.example_es: Necesito ver a un médico—llevo tres días enfermo.
words.example_en: I need to see a doctor—I've been sick for three days.

words.english: My ... hurts / I have pain in ...
words.notes: Essential phrase for describing pain. 'Me duele la cabeza' = my head hurts, 'Me duele el estómago' = my stomach hurts.
words.example_es: Me duele mucho la rodilla desde ayer.
words.example_en: My knee has been hurting a lot since yesterday.

words.notes: Pharmacies in Mexico often have a doctor on duty. Many medications available without a prescription.
words.example_es: ¿Hay una farmacia cerca de aquí?
words.example_en: Is there a pharmacy nearby?

words.english: Pozole (hominy stew with pork or chicken)
words.notes: A traditional Mexican soup/stew very popular in Jalisco, especially on weekends and celebrations.
words.example_es: Los jueves hay pozole en ese restaurante del centro.
words.example_en: On Thursdays there's pozole at that restaurant in the center.

words.notes: The world-famous spirit is from Jalisco! The town of Tequila is about 1.5 hours from Ajijic.
words.example_es: Jalisco es la cuna del tequila.
words.example_en: Jalisco is the birthplace of tequila.

words.notes: The Ajijic mercado municipal is a covered market selling fresh produce, meat, and household goods.
words.example_es: El mercado abre todos los días a las siete.
words.example_en: The market opens every day at seven.

words.english: Could I have...? / May I have...? (polite request)
words.notes: Literally 'Will you gift me...?' — a uniquely Mexican polite way to ask for something at a counter or shop.
words.example_es: ¿Me regala una bolsa, por favor?
words.example_en: Could I have a bag, please?

words.notes: Popular Mexican entertainment. Occasional lucha libre events are held in the Chapala area.
words.example_es: Esta noche hay lucha libre en Chapala.
words.example_en: Tonight there's Mexican wrestling in Chapala.

words.notes: The central plaza of a Mexican town. The zócalo of Ajijic is the social heart of the community.
words.example_es: Nos vemos en el zócalo a las seis.
words.example_en: Let's meet at the main plaza at six.

words.notes: The colonial-era parish church of San Andrés Apóstol is central to life in Ajijic.
words.example_es: La parroquia de San Andrés tiene una arquitectura hermosa.
words.example_en: The Saint Andrew's parish church has beautiful architecture.

words.english: The Ojo de Agua (natural spring/water park)
words.notes: A popular natural spring recreational area near Ajijic.
words.example_es: Los niños adoran nadar en el Ojo de Agua.
words.example_en: Kids love swimming at the Ojo de Agua.

words.notes: The godparent system (compadrazgo) is central to Mexican social structure. Being someone's padrino/madrina carries real social obligations.
words.example_es: Me pidieron ser padrino de la boda.
words.example_en: They asked me to be the wedding godfather/sponsor.

words.notes: In Mexico, 'nieve' often refers to traditional sorbet-style frozen desserts, not just snow.
words.example_es: Vamos por una nieve de limón después del paseo.
words.example_en: Let's get a lime sorbet after the walk.

words.notes: Michoacán and Jalisco are major avocado-producing regions. Avocados are fresh and affordable locally.
words.example_es: Los aguacates aquí son mucho mejores que en el norte.
words.example_en: The avocados here are much better than up north.

words.notes: Mexican paletas come in incredible fresh fruit flavors. The paleta carts are common on Ajijic's streets.
words.example_es: ¿Quieres una paleta de mango con chile?
words.example_en: Do you want a mango chili popsicle?

words.notes: Both 'carro' and 'coche' are used in Mexico. 'Carro' is more common in northern Mexico; 'coche' more in Jalisco.
words.example_es: Dejé el coche en el estacionamiento del mercado.
words.example_en: I left the car in the market parking lot.

words.notes: Three-wheeled motorcycle taxis (also called 'mototaxis' or 'triciclos') are common in the Lake Chapala area.
words.example_es: Toma un mototaxi al centro—es más rápido.
words.example_en: Take a mototaxi to the center—it's faster.

words.notes: Dealing with plumbing issues is a common experience for homeowners in Ajijic.
words.example_es: Necesitamos llamar a un plomero—hay una fuga.
words.example_en: We need to call a plumber—there's a leak.
